title: Car Loans & Leases
description: The payment, the term, the add-ons, and whether you end up owning the car.
wolfLine: The monthly payment is the bait. The total is the hook.

down-payment.definition: Cash you pay up front so you borrow less.
down-payment.example: A $16,000 car with $2,000 down means you borrow $14,000.

car-lease.definition: A deal where you pay to use a car for a set number of months, then give it back. You do not own it at the end.
car-lease.example: $250 a month for 36 months is $9,000 to drive the car, and then you hand the keys back.

upside-down.definition: Owing more on a car than the car is worth.
upside-down.example: You owe $11,000. The car is worth $8,000. You are upside down by $3,000.

lessons.title: What the Car Really Costs
lessons.summary: Price on the window, plus every payment after it.

steps.prompt: You borrow $16,000 and pay $380 a month for 48 months. What do the payments add up to?
How much of that is interest?
Add a $2,000 down payment you already paid. How much cash left you in total?
Which number is the real cost of the purchase?
choices: Every payment, plus the down payment
The monthly payment alone
The price before tax
steps.explain: The monthly number is the bait.

steps.prompt: A car priced at $16,000 costs $16,000 if you finance it.
steps.explain: Interest sits on top. This loan added $2,240.

steps.prompt: Interest is the total of the payments minus the ___.
choices: principal
down payment
tax
steps.explain: You borrowed $16,000. That is the principal in this loan.

lessons.title: Shorter Loan, Smaller Total
lessons.summary: Stretch the loan and the payment shrinks. The interest does the opposite.

steps.context: Same car, same amount borrowed. More months means more interest.
steps.prompt: The 4-year loan: how much interest on $16,000?
The 6-year loan: how much interest?
How much extra interest does the longer loan cost?
The 6-year payment is $80 smaller. Why can it still be the worse deal?
choices: You pay $3,360 more interest
The 6-year loan costs less overall, since each payment is smaller
The car costs less on the long loan
why: Smaller payments, but 24 more of them.
steps.explain: $300 looks easier. The total is $21,600 instead of $18,240.

steps.prompt: Pick the longest loan whenever the monthly payment is the only number you can see.
steps.explain: See the total before you pick the term.

steps.prompt: You can afford $380. What is the careful choice?
choices: The shorter loan, if the $380 fits after needs
The longer loan, to keep cash “free” for more spending
Skip the total and sign
steps.explain: If the higher payment fits, you buy the same car for less.

lessons.title: The Down Payment
lessons.summary: Cash now, less borrowed, less interest later.

steps.context: A [[down payment]] is cash at the start. On a $16,000 car, $2,000 down means the [[principal]] is $14,000, not $16,000.
steps.prompt: What does a down payment do?
choices: It cuts the amount you have to borrow
It raises the interest rate
It is a fee the dealer keeps on top of the price
steps.explain: You pay cash so the loan is smaller.

steps.prompt: Price $18,000. Down payment $3,000. How much do you borrow?
You borrow that $15,000 at 6% simple interest for 1 year, as a rough look. How much interest?
Same rate and year with no down payment, borrowing the full $18,000. How much interest?
How much interest does the $3,000 down payment save in that rough year?
A down payment is wasted money because you could have financed the whole price.
steps.explain: It is money you were going to pay anyway, and it shrinks the interest.

lessons.title: Buy or Lease
lessons.summary: A lease rents the car. A loan is a path to owning it.

steps.context: A [[lease|car-lease]] (the car kind) is paying to drive a car for a set term, then returning it. Miles over the limit cost extra. A loan ends with a car you own, if you finish the payments.
steps.prompt: At the end of a lease, what do you usually have?
choices: Nothing. You give the car back
The car, free and clear
A second car
steps.explain: You paid for the use, not the title.

steps.prompt: A lease is $250 a month for 36 months. How much do you pay to use the car?
A loan is $320 a month for 48 months. How much do you pay?
The lease costs less cash over its term. What do you not get?
choices: Ownership. You hand the car back
The right to drive it during the lease
A monthly payment
steps.explain: $9,000 of driving, then no car. The loan costs more and leaves you the car.

steps.prompt: Going over the mileage limit on a lease can cost an extra fee per mile.
steps.explain: The cheap payment assumes you stay under the cap.

steps.prompt: You drive 18,000 miles a year and the lease allows 10,000. What is the risk?
choices: A big mileage bill when you return it
Nothing. Limits are suggestions
The loan gets cheaper
steps.explain: Match the contract to how you actually drive.

lessons.title: Dealer Add-Ons
lessons.summary: Tap the charge you never agreed to.

steps.context: A buyer’s order should match the deal you discussed. Extra packages are easy to bury in the total.

doc.title: Buyer’s order
doc.subtitle: You did not ask for paint protection

steps.prompt: Which line is the add-on you did not ask for?
steps.explain: Paint protection, $799, was not part of the car you agreed to buy.

doc.title: Buyer’s order
doc.subtitle: You did not ask for paint protection

steps.prompt: How much is the paint protection?
steps.explain: The line says $799.

steps.prompt: What would the total be without that $799?
The dealer says the package is “already on the car.” What can you do?
choices: Ask for it to be removed from the contract before you sign
You must pay it
Drive away and let them bill you later
steps.explain: Before you sign, the line can come off. After you sign, it is yours.

steps.prompt: A document fee and an unwanted protection package are the same kind of charge.
steps.explain: A filing fee can be ordinary. A $799 package you did not ask for is optional, and optional means you can say no.

steps.prompt: Where do you catch this?
choices: On the buyer’s order, before your signature
A month later, on a guess
Never. Add-ons are free
steps.explain: Read every line. The total is not the only number.

lessons.title: Upside Down
lessons.summary: The loan can outlive the car’s value.

steps.context: You are [[upside down]] when the balance is higher than the car’s value. Sell it and you still owe the gap. A long loan and a small down payment get you there faster.
steps.prompt: What does upside down mean on a car loan?
choices: You owe more than the car is worth
The car is paid off
You have equity
steps.explain: The loan is heavier than the car.

steps.prompt: You owe $11,000. The car is worth $8,000. How much is the gap?
You owe $12,500 and the car is worth $13,000. You are upside down.
steps.explain: The car is worth $500 more than the loan. Upside down means the loan is bigger.

steps.prompt: You sell the car for $8,000 and still owe $11,000. What happens?
choices: You still owe the $3,000 gap
The loan disappears with the car
The buyer pays the gap for you
steps.explain: Selling the car does not sell the rest of the loan.

steps.prompt: Which habit makes upside-down less likely?
choices: A bigger down payment and a shorter loan
Zero down and a 7-year term
Rolling an old loan into the new one
steps.explain: Borrow less, and pay it off before the car’s value falls past it.

steps.prompt: You are $3,000 upside down and the dealer offers to add that gap onto a new loan. How much extra principal are you dragging forward?
steps.explain: The whole $3,000. The new car starts life already partly unpaid.

lessons.title: Refinancing the Car
lessons.summary: A lower rate helps. A longer term can give the savings back.

steps.prompt: Your payment is $320. A new loan would be $280. How much a month do you keep?
How much is that over a year?
The new loan is cheaper each month because it lasts two extra years. What else must you check?
choices: The total you will pay, not just the $40
Nothing. A smaller payment is always cheaper
Only the new interest rate
steps.explain: A longer loan can cost more interest even when the payment drops.

steps.prompt: Refinancing makes sense when the new loan’s total cost is lower, and the payment still fits.
steps.explain: Rate, term, and fees. All three.

steps.prompt: The new lender charges a $200 fee. After a year of saving $480, how much are you ahead of that fee?
steps.explain: $480 − $200 = $280. Still ahead, if you keep the loan long enough to get there.

steps.prompt: You are upside down and the new lender says no. What is a reasonable next step?
choices: Keep the current loan and pay extra toward it
Skip payments until they say yes
Trade the car in and roll the gap again
steps.explain: Extra principal is a refinance you give yourself.

lessons.title: Sofia Buys Used
lessons.summary: She can own the car. The package is optional.

story.title: The used car
story.body:
Sofia finds a used car for **$12,000**. She has **$2,000** saved for a down payment, so she would borrow **$10,000**. The lender offers **48** payments of **$230**.

A dealer also waves a **$699** protection package and a 72-month loan with a smaller payment. She wants the car for work, and she wants to own it.

steps.prompt: How much interest is in the 48 payments of $230?
Add the $2,000 down payment. How much does Sofia pay for the $12,000 car, before the package?
What does the $699 package do to the deal if she did not ask for it?
choices: It adds $699 she can refuse before signing
It is required by law
It lowers the interest
steps.explain: Optional means optional.

steps.prompt: The 72-month offer is automatically cheaper because the payment is smaller.
steps.explain: A longer term often adds interest. She should see the total.

steps.prompt: She pays an extra $50 a month on the $230 loan. How much principal does that extra $50 cut in one month?
steps.explain: $50. Extra, on top of the payment, goes to principal.

steps.prompt: She needs the car for work and can afford $230. What fits the goal of owning it?
choices: The 48-month loan, $2,000 down, no package she did not ask for
The longest loan and every package
A lease that ends with no car
steps.explain: Shorter loan, real down payment, no extras.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Car Loans & Leases
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Borrow $9,000. Pay $250 a month for 48 months. How much interest is that?
A $14,000 car with $4,000 down. How much do you borrow?
At the end of a car lease you usually own the car.
steps.explain: You give it back, unless you pay extra to buy it.

steps.prompt: You owe $7,500 and the car is worth $6,000. What are you?
choices: Upside down by $1,500
Ahead by $1,500
Paid off
steps.explain: $7,500 − $6,000 = $1,500 still owed above the car’s value.
